meta.note: Seed glossary. Grows as each unit's key-terms box is authored. Feeds SRS flashcards and programmatic SEO pages. All definitions original — DRAFT until reviewed.

terms.definition: The California state agency that licenses and regulates real estate salespersons and brokers and approves pre-licensing courses.
The appointed head of the California DRE who enforces the Real Estate Law and issues regulations that carry the force of law.
A licensee who may perform licensed real estate activities only while employed by and supervised by a responsible broker.
A licensee authorized to operate a real estate business, employ salespersons, and represent clients directly for compensation.
A trademarked designation for a licensee who is a member of the National Association of Realtors; not all licensees are Realtors®.
Recognition of another state's real estate license; California has no license reciprocity with any state.
Land, anything affixed to it, anything appurtenant to it, and that which is immovable by law — the land plus the bundle of rights.
Movable property (chattel) that is not real property; it transfers by bill of sale rather than by deed.
An item of personal property that has become real property by being attached to land or improvements, judged by tests like MARIA.
Memory aid for the fixture tests: Method of attachment, Adaptability, Relationship of the parties, Intention, and Agreement.
An item installed by a business tenant for use in its trade; unlike ordinary fixtures, the tenant may remove it before the lease ends.
A right or improvement that runs with the land and transfers automatically with it, such as an easement benefiting the parcel or mineral rights.
Annual crops produced by labor (like strawberries or row crops); treated as the tenant farmer's personal property even after a tenancy ends.
The water rights of an owner whose land borders a flowing watercourse such as a river or stream.
The water rights of an owner whose land borders a non-flowing body of water such as a lake or the ocean.
The collection of ownership rights in real property: possession, use, enjoyment, encumbrance (exclusion), and disposition.
The greatest estate in land — ownership of indefinite duration, freely transferable and inheritable, subject only to public and private restrictions.
A fee estate that can be lost if a stated condition is violated, such as land granted 'so long as' it is used for a school.
A freehold estate whose duration is measured by someone's lifetime; the life tenant may use the property but not commit waste.
The future interest held by a third party who takes title when a life estate ends.
The future interest retained by a grantor who takes the property back when a lesser estate (like a life estate) ends.
A leasehold with a definite start and end date; it terminates automatically without notice.
A leasehold that renews automatically period to period (like month-to-month) until either party gives proper notice.
A tenancy with no fixed term that either party may end at any time (with statutory notice in California).
The interest of a tenant who lawfully took possession but stays after the right to possession has ended — a holdover tenant.
Ownership by one person or entity alone — sole ownership, with interests 'severed' from everyone else.
Co-ownership with right of survivorship requiring the four unities of time, title, interest, and possession.
Co-ownership in undivided shares (which may be unequal) with no right of survivorship; each owner's share passes to their heirs.
Property acquired by California spouses during marriage through the labor of either; each spouse owns an equal, undivided one-half interest.
The feature of joint tenancy (and community property with right of survivorship) by which a deceased co-owner's interest passes automatically to the surviving co-owner(s).
A co-owner's fractional interest in the whole property, entitling them to possession of all of it, not a physically divided piece.
A lawsuit by a co-owner asking a court to divide co-owned property or order it sold and split the proceeds.
Any claim, lien, charge, or liability attached to real property that limits or burdens it, such as easements, liens, or restrictions.
A money encumbrance — a charge against property making it security for a debt, such as a trust deed, tax lien, or judgment lien.
A statutory lien available to contractors, subcontractors, laborers, and material suppliers who improve property and are not paid.
An involuntary, general lien created by recording an abstract of judgment against the debtor's property in the county.
A recorded notice of pending litigation affecting title to or possession of real property, clouding title until the suit resolves.
A non-possessory right to use another person's land for a specific purpose, such as a driveway or utility line.
An easement that benefits a neighboring parcel (the dominant tenement) and runs with the land when either parcel is sold.
An easement that benefits a person or company rather than a parcel of land — utility easements are the classic example.
The parcel of land that benefits from an easement appurtenant.
The parcel of land that is burdened by an easement — the land the easement crosses.
Acquiring an easement by open, notorious, hostile, and continuous use of another's land for five years in California.
A physical intrusion of a structure or improvement onto a neighbor's land, such as a fence built over the boundary line.
Covenants, conditions, and restrictions — recorded private restrictions that control how property in a subdivision or common-interest development may be used.
A revocable, personal permission to use another's land that, unlike an easement, creates no interest in the land.
The relationship in which one person (the agent) represents another (the principal) in dealings with third parties.
A person in a position of trust and confidence who owes their principal utmost care, integrity, honesty, and loyalty.
The person who authorizes an agent to represent them — in a listing, the seller; in a buyer representation agreement, the buyer.
Memory aid for fiduciary duties: Obedience, Loyalty, Disclosure, Confidentiality, Accounting, and Reasonable care.
One brokerage representing both buyer and seller in the same transaction; lawful in California only with the informed written consent of both.
Agency created by the principal's conduct causing a third party to reasonably believe someone is their agent, even without an express agreement.
Approval of an act after the fact — a principal accepting the benefits of an unauthorized act creates agency by ratification.
An agent of an agent — a person authorized to help perform the agency, owing the same duties to the principal.
Any undisclosed compensation or benefit an agent gains from the agency; taking one violates the duty of loyalty and is grounds for discipline.
A non-factual, exaggerated sales statement of opinion ('best view in Pasadena') that a reasonable buyer would not rely on as fact.
A false statement of material fact; if intentional it is fraud, and even innocent misrepresentation can allow rescission.
A legally enforceable agreement requiring capable parties, mutual consent, lawful object, and consideration.
A proposal showing contractual intent, definite terms, and communication to the offeree, which the offeree can accept to form a contract.
The offeree's unqualified agreement to the offer's terms, communicated in the manner required by the offer.
A response that changes the terms of an offer; it rejects and terminates the original offer and becomes a new offer.
Something of value exchanged by each party — money, a promise, or forbearance — required for a valid contract.
The law (Civil Code §1624) requiring certain contracts, including those for the sale of real property, to be in writing to be enforceable.
An agreement with no legal effect at all, such as a contract for an illegal purpose.
A contract valid on its face that one party (such as a minor or a defrauded party) may elect to rescind.
A contract that may be valid between the parties but that a court will not enforce, such as an oral real estate sale agreement.
A contract in which something remains to be performed — a purchase agreement is executory until closing.
A contract fully performed by both parties; also used loosely to mean 'signed.'
A remedy that cancels the contract and restores the parties to their pre-contract positions, returning consideration paid.
An amount the parties agree in advance will serve as damages for breach; in California residential purchases, capped at 3% of the price for the buyer's deposit.
A court order compelling a breaching party to perform the contract; available for real estate because land is unique.
Substituting a new contract or a new party for an old one, with intent to extinguish the original obligation.
Transferring one's rights under a contract to another person; the assignor remains secondarily liable unless there is a novation.
A contract that keeps an offer open — the optionor sells the optionee the right, for consideration, to buy at set terms within a set time.
A condition (like financing, appraisal, or inspection) that must be satisfied or waived before a party is obligated to close.
A listing under which the broker earns the commission no matter who procures the buyer — even if the owner sells it themselves.
A listing under which the broker is the only agent, but the owner may sell without paying a commission.
A non-exclusive listing given to any number of brokers; only the broker who procures the buyer earns a commission.
A listing provision entitling the broker to a commission if, within a stated period after expiration, the owner sells to a buyer the broker introduced.
A contract clause making stated deadlines strict, so late performance is a material breach.
The statutory form on which a California residential seller discloses the property's known condition and defects to the buyer.
The statutory disclosure identifying whether property lies in mapped hazard zones such as flood, fire severity, or earthquake fault zones.
Any fact that would affect a reasonable person's decision to buy or the price they would pay; agents must disclose material facts they know.
A sale term meaning the seller won't repair or credit for known conditions; it does not eliminate California disclosure duties.
Property psychologically impacted by an event such as a death; California limits required disclosure of deaths to those within three years, with exceptions.
The statutorily required notice in sales contracts about the public sex-offender database maintained by the Department of Justice.
A neutral third-party arrangement in which a depository holds funds and documents and closes the transaction per the parties' mutual instructions.
The escrow holder's role: a dual agent of both parties for carrying out instructions, favoring neither.
The recorded history of successive ownership of a property, traced through public records.
Title reasonably free from doubt and defects that a prudent buyer would accept.
The title company's report of the current condition of title — vesting, liens, and exceptions — offered before issuing a policy.
The standard California title insurance policy, typically protecting the owner against recorded defects and matters of public record.
The extended-coverage title policy, typically required by lenders, that adds protection for off-record matters like unrecorded liens and survey issues.
California's usual deed, carrying two implied warranties: the grantor has not already conveyed the property and has disclosed known encumbrances.
A deed conveying whatever interest the grantor has, if any, with no warranties at all.
Filing a document with the county recorder, giving constructive notice of its contents to the world and establishing priority.
Notice imputed by law — from recorded documents or from possession of the property — whether or not a person actually knows.
Knowledge a person actually has, however acquired.
A formal declaration before a notary that a signature is genuine and voluntary; required before a deed can be recorded.
The borrower's written promise to repay a debt; the evidence of the debt that the security instrument secures.
California's dominant security instrument, involving a trustor (borrower), beneficiary (lender), and trustee holding bare legal title with power of sale.
The borrower under a deed of trust, who conveys bare legal title to the trustee as security for the loan.
The neutral third party under a deed of trust who holds bare legal title and may sell the property upon default via the power of sale.
The lender under a deed of trust, for whose benefit the property is held as security.
The clause in a deed of trust authorizing the trustee to sell the property non-judicially after default, following statutory notice periods.
The borrower's right to cure a default by paying the missed amounts (plus costs) and continue the loan, available until shortly before the trustee's sale.
The borrower voluntarily deeding the property to the lender to avoid foreclosure; the lender takes subject to junior liens.
A provision letting the lender declare the entire balance due upon default.
A provision letting the lender call the loan due if the borrower transfers the property.
A judgment against a borrower for the shortfall after a foreclosure sale; barred in California after non-judicial foreclosure and for standard purchase-money loans.
The loan amount divided by the lesser of price or appraised value; higher LTV means more leverage and more lender risk.
The four components of a typical housing payment: principal, interest, taxes, and insurance.
Prepaid interest charged at closing — one point equals 1% of the loan amount — used to buy down the rate or increase lender yield.
The cost of credit expressed as a yearly rate including certain fees, disclosed under the Truth in Lending Act.
Repaying a loan through regular payments that cover interest and gradually reduce principal to zero at maturity.
A conventional loan meeting Fannie Mae/Freddie Mac purchase standards, including the loan-size limit.
Insurance protecting a conventional lender against borrower default, generally required when LTV exceeds 80%.
Junior financing in which the new lender's note wraps the existing loan; the borrower pays the wrap lender, who keeps paying the underlying loan.
Credit the seller extends to the buyer, secured by the property being sold.
The most probable price a property should bring in an open, competitive market with informed parties acting prudently and without duress.
The idea that a buyer will pay no more for a property than the cost of acquiring an equally desirable substitute — the foundation of the sales comparison approach.
The legally permissible, physically possible, financially feasible use that produces the greatest value.
Valuing property by adjusting recent sales of comparable properties for differences; the primary approach for houses.
Valuing property as land value plus replacement cost of improvements minus depreciation; most reliable for new or special-purpose buildings.
Valuing property by capitalizing its net operating income: value = NOI ÷ capitalization rate.
The rate of return used to convert net operating income to value; higher cap rates mean lower values for the same income.
A shortcut ratio — price divided by gross rent — used to estimate the value of rental property from its rent.
Loss in value from any cause: physical deterioration, functional obsolescence, or external (economic) obsolescence.
Loss in value from outdated or poor design — a one-bath five-bedroom house, for example.
Loss in value from factors outside the property, such as a new freeway ramp next door; it is incurable.
A licensee's pricing analysis using comparable sales; it is not an appraisal, which only a licensed appraiser can perform.
The appraiser's weighing of the value indications from the three approaches into a final opinion of value.
The government's inherent power to regulate for public health, safety, morals, and welfare — the basis of zoning — without compensation.
The government's power to take private property for public use upon payment of just compensation, through condemnation.
An owner's action against the government when its activity has effectively taken or damaged property without formal condemnation.
Permission to deviate from a zoning standard (like a setback) due to a parcel's special hardship; not a change of use classification.
A lawful use that predates a zoning change and may continue ('grandfathered') though it no longer conforms.
Permission for a use zoning allows only upon special approval and conditions, like a church or school in a residential zone.
A group protected from housing discrimination — federally: race, color, religion, sex, national origin, disability, familial status; California adds more (e.g., source of income).
Channeling homebuyers toward or away from neighborhoods based on a protected characteristic; illegal.
Inducing owners to sell by suggesting members of a protected class are moving into the neighborhood (panic selling); illegal.
Refusing to lend or insure in an area based on its demographics rather than the applicant's qualifications; illegal.
The protected class covering households with children under 18, pregnant persons, and those securing custody.
California law prohibiting discrimination by all business establishments — including brokerages and landlords.
California's Fair Employment and Housing Act, the state's primary fair-housing statute, broader than the federal act.
'According to value' — property taxes are ad valorem taxes based on assessed value.
The California constitutional limit capping the basic property tax rate at 1% of assessed value with assessment increases limited to 2% per year until a change of ownership.
A county (and sometimes city) tax on transferring real property, commonly $0.55 per $500 of consideration at the county level.
The owner's investment in property for tax purposes — generally cost plus improvements — used to measure gain on sale.
A tax-deferred exchange of like-kind investment or business real property under Internal Revenue Code §1031.
Non-like-kind value (cash or debt relief) received in a 1031 exchange; taxable to the extent of gain.

Money or things of value received by a licensee on behalf of another in a transaction — deposits, rents — which must be placed in neutral escrow, a trust account, or the owner's hands within three business days.
Mixing trust funds with the licensee's own funds — a license-discipline violation even without loss to anyone.
Misappropriating trust funds — actually using client money; more serious than commingling and criminally chargeable.
Dividing ongoing expenses (taxes, rents, HOA dues) between buyer and seller as of closing, typically using a 30-day month/360-day year unless agreed otherwise.
A lender-held account collecting monthly installments toward property taxes and insurance with each loan payment.
California's summary court action by which a landlord recovers possession from a tenant after proper notice.
A landlord's breach that makes the premises unusable, allowing the tenant to move out and end the lease without further liability.
Electronic fingerprinting submitted with a California license application so the Department of Justice and FBI can complete a background check.
A valid real estate license not associated with an employing broker; the licensee may not perform licensed activity until a broker sponsors them.
A license issued or continued after discipline subject to conditions such as working for a named broker, filing reports, posting a bond, or serving probation.
A private cooperative listing database operated by associations of Realtors®, not a government registry; access generally requires association membership.
Factory-built housing that is personal property when registered with HCD on rented space, and becomes real property when placed on a permanent foundation on owned land as provided by statute.
A UCC financing statement recorded against real property to perfect a security interest in goods that have become fixtures — leased solar systems are a common example.
Another name for personal property; chattel loans finance personal property at different rates and terms than real property mortgages.
Attaching personal property to land so that it becomes real property, such as lumber built into a deck.
Detaching something from real property — crops, fixtures, minerals — so that it becomes personal property.
Acquiring property by its addition to property you already own, such as trade fixtures a tenant abandons after the tenancy ends.
Naturally occurring growth such as native trees and grasses; part of the real property until severed.
